Section: General
Corrected Study Guide for RAG Retrieval
Contents
Purpose: a structured study guide designed for topic-wise learning and retrieval practice.

Section: Introduction to SQL Joins
A SQL join combines rows from two tables using a related column or a join condition. Joins let you query normalized
data without storing the same fact repeatedly.
SELECT s.student_id, s.name, e.course_id
JOIN Enrollments AS e
Use explicit JOIN ... ON syntax. It makes the relationship visible and avoids the accidental Cartesian products that old
comma-join syntax can produce.

Section: Sample Tables
Students
student_id | name
1 | Asha
2 | Ravi
3 | Meera
Enrollments
student_id | course
1 | SQL
2 | Python
4 | Java
The sample deliberately includes student 3 without an enrollment and enrollment 4 without a matching student. Those
unmatched rows make outer-join behavior easier to see.

Section: INNER JOIN
INNER JOIN returns only rows that satisfy the join condition in both tables.
INNER JOIN Enrollments AS e
Expected matches: Asha with SQL and Ravi with Python. Meera and the enrollment for student 4 are excluded.

Section: LEFT JOIN
LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and matching rows from the right table. If there is no match, right-side
columns are NULL.
LEFT JOIN Enrollments AS e
Meera remains in the output with NULL for course. A frequent mistake is putting a right-table filter in WHERE when
unmatched left rows should remain; that can turn the result into inner-join-like behavior.

Section: RIGHT JOIN
RIGHT JOIN returns every row from the right table and matching rows from the left table. Unmatched left-side columns
are NULL.
RIGHT JOIN Enrollments AS e
The enrollment for student 4 remains, with NULL student details. Many teams prefer rewriting RIGHT JOIN as LEFT
JOIN by swapping table order for readability.

Section: FULL OUTER JOIN
FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched rows plus unmatched rows from both sides. Unmatched columns are filled with
NULL.
MySQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN as a direct keyword. A common MySQL pattern combines a LEFT JOIN
with a RIGHT-only set using UNION ALL.
LEFT JOIN Enrollments AS e
ON s.student_id = e.student_id
UNION ALL
RIGHT JOIN Enrollments AS e
ON s.student_id = e.student_id
WHERE s.student_id IS NULL;
The second branch keeps only right-side rows without a left-side match. UNION ALL avoids unnecessary duplicate
elimination; the anti-match condition prevents matched rows from appearing twice.

Section: CROSS JOIN
CROSS JOIN returns every combination of rows. If the left table has m rows and the right table has n rows, the result
has m × n rows.
SELECT s.name, c.course_name
CROSS JOIN Courses AS c;

Section: Self join
A self join joins a table to itself, often to represent hierarchies such as employees and managers.
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM Employees AS e
LEFT JOIN Employees AS m
ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;

Section: Join Conditions and NULL
Use ON to state how rows relate; use WHERE to filter the joined result.
NULL does not equal NULL under ordinary equality comparison. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
One-to-many joins can multiply rows. Check the relationship cardinality before interpreting counts.
Use qualified names such as s.student_id when multiple tables share column names.
For an outer join, a filter on the optional side in WHERE may remove rows with NULLs. Consider putting that filter in
ON when preserving unmatched rows is required.

Section: Comparison at a Glance
Join
Rows returned
INNER
Only matching rows
LEFT
All left rows, plus right matches
RIGHT
All right rows, plus left matches
FULL OUTER
All rows from both sides, matched where possible
CROSS
Every left/right combination
SELF
A table joined to itself; type depends on chosen join

Section: Common Mistakes
Forgetting the ON condition and creating a huge Cartesian result.
Joining on a non-unique column and unexpectedly multiplying rows.
Using = NULL instead of IS NULL.
Filtering right-side columns in WHERE and unintentionally losing LEFT JOIN unmatched rows.
Assuming MySQL accepts FULL OUTER JOIN directly.
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL without considering duplicate-removal cost and semantics.

Section: Interview Practice
Return every student, including those without an enrollment. Which join is suitable?
Return enrollments even when the student record is missing. Which join is suitable?
Explain the difference between ON and WHERE for an outer join.
Write a MySQL query that emulates FULL OUTER JOIN.
What is the maximum number of rows produced by a CROSS JOIN of 7 and 4 rows?
Why might a join return more rows than the left table?
